claim: Recent genome analyses have identified recurrent mutations in the cohesin complex in a wide range of human cancers.
source: Recent genome analyses have identified recurrent mutations in the cohesin complex in a wide range of human cancers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: STAG2 displays a strong synthetic lethal interaction with its paralog STAG1.
source: Here we demonstrate that the most frequently mutated subunit of the cohesin complex, STAG2, displays a strong synthetic lethal interaction with its paralog STAG1.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including siRNA screens, CRISPR/Cas9 experiments, and competition assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: STAG1 loss abrogates sister chromatid cohesion in STAG2 mutated but not in wild-type cells.
source: Mechanistically, STAG1 loss abrogates sister chromatid cohesion in STAG2 mutated but not in wild-type cells leading to mitotic catastrophe, defective cell division and apoptosis.
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by chromosome spread analysis shown in Figure 2C demonstrating loss of sister chromatid cohesion.

claim: STAG1 loss in STAG2 mutated cells leads to mitotic catastrophe, defective cell division and apoptosis.
source: Mechanistically, STAG1 loss abrogates sister chromatid cohesion in STAG2 mutated but not in wild-type cells leading to mitotic catastrophe, defective cell division and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased mitotic index, prolonged mitosis duration, chromosome misalignment (Figure 2A, 2B), and increased caspase activity (Figure 2D).

claim: STAG1 inactivation inhibits the proliferation of STAG2 mutated but not wild-type bladder cancer cell lines.
source: STAG1 inactivation inhibits the proliferation of STAG2 mutated but not wild-type bladder cancer and Ewing sarcoma cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by viability assays across a panel of 16 bladder cancer cell lines shown in Figure 3B.

claim: STAG1 inactivation inhibits the proliferation of STAG2 mutated but not wild-type Ewing sarcoma cell lines.
source: STAG1 inactivation inhibits the proliferation of STAG2 mutated but not wild-type bladder cancer and Ewing sarcoma cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by viability assays across a panel of 4 Ewing sarcoma cell lines shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Restoration of STAG2 expression in a mutated bladder cancer model alleviates the dependency on STAG1.
source: Restoration of STAG2 expression in a mutated bladder cancer model alleviates the dependency on STAG1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments in UM-UC-3 cells expressing FLAG-STAG2 transgene shown in Figure 3G.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 support sister chromatid cohesion to redundantly ensure cell survival.
source: Thus, STAG1 and STAG2 support sister chromatid cohesion to redundantly ensure cell survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality data and mechanistic studies showing that loss of both paralogs abrogates cohesion.

claim: STAG1 represents a vulnerability of cancer cells carrying mutations in STAG2 across different cancer contexts.
source: STAG1 represents a vulnerability of cancer cells carrying mutations in the major emerging tumor suppressor STAG2 across different cancer contexts.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple cancer types including colon carcinoma, leukemia, bladder cancer, and Ewing sarcoma.

claim: Cohesin is a highly conserved ring-shaped protein complex that topologically embraces chromatid fibers.
source: Cohesin is a highly conserved ring-shaped protein complex that is thought to topologically embrace chromatid fibers (Peters and Nishiyama, 2012), which is essential for sister chromatid cohesion and chromosome segregation in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Peters and Nishiyama, 2012).

claim: Cohesin is essential for sister chromatid cohesion and chromosome segregation in eukaryotes.
source: Cohesin is a highly conserved ring-shaped protein complex that is thought to topologically embrace chromatid fibers (Peters and Nishiyama, 2012), which is essential for sister chromatid cohesion and chromosome segregation in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: Cohesin participates in DNA repair, genome organization and gene expression.
source: In addition, cohesin participates in DNA repair, genome organization and gene expression (Losada, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Losada, 2014).

claim: The cohesin subunits SMC1, SMC3 and RAD21 comprise the core ring of the complex.
source: The cohesin subunits SMC1, SMC3 and RAD21 (also called SCC1) comprise the core ring of the complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cohesin structure.

claim: A HEAT repeat protein of the Scc3/STAG family peripherally associates with the core cohesin ring by binding to RAD21.
source: A fourth universally conserved subunit, a HEAT repeat protein of the Scc3/STAG family, peripherally associates with the core cohesin ring by binding to RAD21 (Tóth et al., 1999), and is required for the dynamic association of cohesin with chromatin (Hu et al., 2011; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Tóth et al., 1999).

claim: The Scc3/STAG family protein is required for the dynamic association of cohesin with chromatin.
source: A fourth universally conserved subunit, a HEAT repeat protein of the Scc3/STAG family, peripherally associates with the core cohesin ring by binding to RAD21 (Tóth et al., 1999), and is required for the dynamic association of cohesin with chromatin (Hu et al., 2011; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Hu et al., 2011; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2014).

claim: Human somatic cells express two paralogs of the Scc3/STAG protein, called STAG1 and STAG2.
source: Human somatic cells express two paralogs of this protein, called STAG1 and STAG2 (Losada et al., 2000; Sumara et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Losada et al., 2000; Sumara et al., 2000).

claim: Recurrent mutations in cohesin subunits and regulators occur in approximately 7.3% of all human cancers.
source: Recent cancer genome studies identified recurrent mutations in cohesin subunits and regulators in approximately 7.3% of all human cancers (Lawrence et al., 2014; Leiserson et al., 2015; Solomon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cancer genome studies (Lawrence et al., 2014; Leiserson et al., 2015; Solomon et al., 2011).

claim: STAG2 is the most frequently mutated cohesin subunit.
source: STAG2, the most frequently mutated cohesin subunit, emerges as one of only 12 genes that are significantly mutated in four or more major human malignancies (Lawrence et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to cancer genome analysis (Lawrence et al., 2014).

claim: STAG2 is one of only 12 genes that are significantly mutated in four or more major human malignancies.
source: STAG2, the most frequently mutated cohesin subunit, emerges as one of only 12 genes that are significantly mutated in four or more major human malignancies (Lawrence et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to cancer genome analysis (Lawrence et al., 2014).

claim: STAG2 mutations have been reported in ~6% of acute myeloid leukemias and myelodysplastic syndromes.
source: STAG2 mutations have been reported in ~6% of acute myeloid leukemias and myelodysplastic syndromes (Kon et al., 2013; Thota et al., 2014; Walter et al., 2012), 15–22% of Ewing's sarcomas (Brohl et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2014; Tirode et al., 2014), and in up to 26% of bladder cancers of various stages and grades (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Solomon et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Kon et al., 2013; Thota et al., 2014; Walter et al., 2012).

claim: STAG2 mutations have been reported in 15–22% of Ewing's sarcomas.
source: STAG2 mutations have been reported in ~6% of acute myeloid leukemias and myelodysplastic syndromes (Kon et al., 2013; Thota et al., 2014; Walter et al., 2012), 15–22% of Ewing's sarcomas (Brohl et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2014; Tirode et al., 2014), and in up to 26% of bladder cancers of various stages and grades (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Solomon et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Brohl et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2014; Tirode et al., 2014).

claim: STAG2 mutations have been reported in up to 26% of bladder cancers of various stages and grades.
source: STAG2 mutations have been reported in ~6% of acute myeloid leukemias and myelodysplastic syndromes (Kon et al., 2013; Thota et al., 2014; Walter et al., 2012), 15–22% of Ewing's sarcomas (Brohl et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2014; Tirode et al., 2014), and in up to 26% of bladder cancers of various stages and grades (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Solomon et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2013; Solomon et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2014).

claim: The deleterious nature of most STAG2 mutations strongly suggests that the gene represents a new tumor suppressor.
source: The deleterious nature of most STAG2 mutations strongly suggests that the gene represents a new tumor suppressor (Hill et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Hill et al., 2016) and inference from mutation patterns.

claim: STAG2 mutations were initially thought to promote tumorigenesis due to defects in sister chromatid cohesion leading to genome instability.
source: STAG2 mutations were initially thought to promote tumorigenesis due to defects in sister chromatid cohesin leading to genome instability (Barber et al., 2008; Solomon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Barber et al., 2008; Solomon et al., 2011).

claim: The vast majority of cohesin-mutated cancers are euploid.
source: However, the vast majority of cohesin-mutated cancers are euploid (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Kon et al., 2013), indicating that cohesin mutations may promote tumorigenesis through altering different cohesin functions such as genome organization and transcriptional regulation (Galeev et al., 2016; Mazumdar et al., 2015; Mullenders et al., 2015; Viny et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Kon et al., 2013).

claim: Cohesin mutations may promote tumorigenesis through altering genome organization and transcriptional regulation.
source: However, the vast majority of cohesin-mutated cancers are euploid (Balbás-Martínez et al., 2013; Kon et al., 2013), indicating that cohesin mutations may promote tumorigenesis through altering different cohesin functions such as genome organization and transcriptional regulation (Galeev et al., 2016; Mazumdar et al., 2015; Mullenders et al., 2015; Viny et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies (Galeev et al., 2016; Mazumdar et al., 2015; Mullenders et al., 2015; Viny et al., 2015) and inference from the euploid nature of cohesin-mutated cancers.

claim: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors have shown success in the treatment of BRCA-mutated ovarian and prostate cancer.
source: Regardless of the mechanisms driving cohesin mutant tumors, the recent success of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors in the treatment of BRCA-mutated ovarian and prostate cancer demonstrates that exploiting tumor suppressor loss by applying the concept of synthetic lethality in defined patient populations can impact clinical cancer care (Castro et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Mirza et al., 2016; Oza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies (Castro et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Mirza et al., 2016; Oza et al., 2015).

claim: Exploiting tumor suppressor loss by applying the concept of synthetic lethality in defined patient populations can impact clinical cancer care.
source: Regardless of the mechanisms driving cohesin mutant tumors, the recent success of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors in the treatment of BRCA-mutated ovarian and prostate cancer demonstrates that exploiting tumor suppressor loss by applying the concept of synthetic lethality in defined patient populations can impact clinical cancer care (Castro et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Mirza et al., 2016; Oza et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies demonstrating the PARP inhibitor success (Castro et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Mirza et al., 2016; Oza et al., 2015).

claim: An estimated half a million individuals have STAG2-mutant malignancies.
source: The estimated half a million individuals with STAG2-mutant malignancies would greatly profit from exploring specific dependencies of these cancers.
evidence: This is an estimate based on mutation frequencies in various cancers.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 was used to inactivate STAG2 in near-diploid, chromosomally stable HCT 116 colon carcinoma cells.
source: To identify factors whose inactivation would be synthetic lethal with loss of STAG2 function, we first used CRISPR/Cas9 to inactivate STAG2 in near-diploid, chromosomally stable HCT 116 colon carcinoma cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Two HCT 116 clones, STAG2-505c1 and 502c4, harbor deleterious mutations in STAG2 and lack detectable STAG2 protein expression.
source: Two clones, STAG2- 505c1 and 502c4, harboring deleterious mutations in STAG2 and lacking detectable STAG2 protein expression were selected for analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and immunoblotting data.

claim: Depletion of SGOL1 had a detrimental impact on viability of both parental and STAG2- HCT 116 cells.
source: Depletion of the known essential cohesin regulator SGOL1 had a detrimental impact on viability of both parental and STAG2- cells.
evidence: This is supported by the siRNA screen data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Depletion of STAG1 strongly decreased cell viability in STAG2- cells, while being tolerated by the isogenic parental cells.
source: Remarkably, depletion of STAG1 strongly decreased cell viability in STAG2- cells, while being tolerated by the isogenic parental cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the siRNA screen data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of an siRNA-resistant STAG1 transgene alleviated the anti-proliferative effect of STAG1 siRNA in STAG2- HCT 116 cells.
source: Expression of an siRNA-resistant STAG1 transgene alleviated the anti-proliferative effect of STAG1 but not of SGOL1 siRNA duplexes in STAG2- HCT 116 cells demonstrating the specificity of the siRNA treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Double depletion of STAG1 and STAG2 by siRNA in parental cells confirmed their synthetic lethal interaction.
source: Double depletion of STAG1 and STAG2 by siRNA in parental cells confirmed their synthetic lethal interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by double knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The dependency of STAG2- cells on STAG1 was independent of p53.
source: Co-depletion of p53 and STAG1 indicated that the dependency of STAG2- cells on STAG1 was independent of p53 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by co-depletion experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Depletion of STAG1 had no effect on cell viability in non-transformed telomerase-immortalized human retinal pigment epithelial cells (hTERT RPE-1).
source: In contrast to the loss of essential cohesin subunits or regulators, depletion of STAG1 had no effect on cell viability in non-transformed telomerase-immortalized human retinal pigment epithelial cells (hTERT RPE-1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Neither STAG1 nor STAG2 is essential for the proliferation of hTERT-RPE1 cells.
source: This result is supported by a large-scale genetic loss-of-function study that found that neither STAG1 nor STAG2 is essential for the proliferation of hTERT-RPE1 cells (Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a large-scale study (Hart et al., 2015).

claim: Transduction with sgRNAs targeting STAG1 caused the depletion of STAG2- HCT 116 and KBM-7 cells but not of their parental STAG2 proficient counterparts.
source: In striking contrast, transduction with sgRNAs targeting STAG1 caused the depletion of STAG2- HCT 116 and KBM-7 cells but not of their parental STAG2 proficient counterparts (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: STAG1 inactivation has little if any impact on the viability and proliferation of STAG2 wild-type cancer cells and non-transformed cells.
source: STAG1 inactivation has little if any impact on the viability and proliferation of STAG2 wild-type cancer cells and non-transformed cells, but is essential for survival in the absence of STAG2.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple cell lines including hTERT RPE-1 and STAG2 wild-type cancer cells.

claim: STAG1 is essential for survival in the absence of STAG2.
source: STAG1 inactivation has little if any impact on the viability and proliferation of STAG2 wild-type cancer cells and non-transformed cells, but is essential for survival in the absence of STAG2.
evidence: This is supported by synthetic lethality data from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Depletion of STAG1 by siRNA abrogated both cell viability and sister chromatid cohesion in HCT 116 cell clones with patient-derived deleterious STAG2 mutations.
source: STAG1 depletion by siRNA abrogated both cell viability and sister chromatid cohesion in HCT 116 cell clones, in which three patient-derived deleterious mutations had been engineered into the STAG2 locus (Kim et al., 2016), but not in parental HCT 116 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of STAG1 resulted in an increase in the mitotic index in STAG2- but not wild-type HCT 116 cells.
source: Depletion of STAG1 resulted in an increase in the mitotic index and a prolongation of the duration of mitosis in STAG2- but not wild-type cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of STAG1 resulted in a prolongation of the duration of mitosis in STAG2- but not wild-type HCT 116 cells.
source: Depletion of STAG1 resulted in an increase in the mitotic index and a prolongation of the duration of mitosis in STAG2- but not wild-type cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: STAG1 loss resulted in a failure to align chromosomes at the metaphase plate in STAG2- cells.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed a failure to align chromosomes at the metaphase plate upon STAG1 loss in STAG2- cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: STAG2 inactivation caused a partial loss of centromeric cohesion in HCT 116 cells.
source: In mitotic chromosome spread analysis STAG2 inactivation caused a partial loss of centromeric cohesion in HCT 116 cells as previously reported (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Kim et al., 2016; Remeseiro et al., 2012; Solomon et al., 2011) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 2C and citations to prior work (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Kim et al., 2016; Remeseiro et al., 2012; Solomon et al., 2011).

claim: Depletion of SGOL1 resulted in a complete loss of sister chromatid cohesion in most chromosome spreads irrespective of STAG2 genotype.
source: Depletion of the essential centromeric cohesin protection factor SGOL1 resulted in a complete loss of sister chromatid cohesion in most chromosome spreads irrespective of STAG2 genotype.
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: STAG1 depletion selectively abrogated sister chromatid cohesion in STAG2- but not parental HCT 116 cells.
source: In striking contrast, STAG1 depletion selectively abrogated sister chromatid cohesion in STAG2- but not parental cells (Figure 2C, single chromatids).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of STAG1 in STAG2- cells was accompanied by the emergence of aberrantly sized and shaped interphase nuclei.
source: The severe mitotic defects observed upon loss of STAG1 in STAG2- cells were accompanied by the emergence of aberrantly sized and shaped interphase nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and by a progressive increase in apoptosis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by nuclear morphology analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of STAG1 in STAG2- cells was accompanied by a progressive increase in apoptosis.
source: The severe mitotic defects observed upon loss of STAG1 in STAG2- cells were accompanied by the emergence of aberrantly sized and shaped interphase nuclei (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and by a progressive increase in apoptosis (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by caspase activity assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: STAG1 inactivation abrogates sister chromatid cohesion exclusively in STAG2- cells resulting in catastrophic mitotic failure, abnormal cell division and apoptosis.
source: STAG1 inactivation abrogates sister chromatid cohesion exclusively in STAG2- cells resulting in catastrophic mitotic failure, abnormal cell division and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of data including chromosome spreads, mitotic analysis, and apoptosis assays.

claim: To hold sister chromatids together, cohesin can tolerate the loss of either STAG1 or STAG2 alone but not the loss of both.
source: To hold sister chromatids together, cohesin can tolerate the loss of either STAG1 or STAG2 alone but not the loss of both.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality data and mechanistic studies.

claim: The genetic interaction between STAG paralogs is conserved in three major human malignancies: carcinoma, leukemia and sarcoma.
source: Thus, the genetic interaction between STAG paralogs is conserved in three major human malignancies: carcinoma, leukemia and sarcoma.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing the interaction in HCT 116 (carcinoma), KBM-7 (leukemia), bladder cancer (carcinoma), and Ewing sarcoma cells.

claim: Cancer cells harboring deleterious STAG2 mutations remain exquisitely dependent on STAG1.
source: Importantly, the finding that cancer cells harboring deleterious STAG2 mutations remain exquisitely dependent on STAG1 demonstrates that this genetic vulnerability is maintained throughout the process of carcinogenesis and not bypassed by adaptive processes, such as the transcriptional activation of the germline-specific paralog STAG3 (Pezzi et al., 2000; Prieto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by data from patient-derived cell lines with STAG2 mutations.

claim: The genetic vulnerability of STAG2 mutant cells to STAG1 loss is maintained throughout the process of carcinogenesis and not bypassed by adaptive processes.
source: Importantly, the finding that cancer cells harboring deleterious STAG2 mutations remain exquisitely dependent on STAG1 demonstrates that this genetic vulnerability is maintained throughout the process of carcinogenesis and not bypassed by adaptive processes, such as the transcriptional activation of the germline-specific paralog STAG3 (Pezzi et al., 2000; Prieto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that established cancer cell lines with STAG2 mutations still depend on STAG1.

claim: Expression analysis did not reveal upregulation of STAG1 protein or mRNA as a major compensatory mechanism for the loss of STAG2 function in cancer cell lines or patient tumors.
source: Furthermore, expression analysis did not reveal upregulation of STAG1 protein or mRNA as a major compensatory mechanism for the loss of STAG2 function in cancer cell lines or patient tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: STAG2 status represented a predictive marker for the sensitivity to STAG1 depletion across the bladder cancer cell line panel.
source: siRNA experiments revealed that STAG2 status represented a predictive marker for the sensitivity to STAG1 depletion across the bladder cancer cell line panel.
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data across 16 bladder cancer cell lines shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All bladder cancer cell lines in the panel were highly sensitive to depletion of the key mitotic kinase PLK1.
source: Whereas all cell lines were highly sensitive to depletion of the key mitotic kinase PLK1, STAG1 siRNA reduced cell viability in STAG2-negative bladder cancer cells but had little or no effect on STAG2-positive bladder cancer cell lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: STAG1 siRNA reduced cell viability in STAG2-negative bladder cancer cells but had little or no effect on STAG2-positive bladder cancer cell lines.
source: Whereas all cell lines were highly sensitive to depletion of the key mitotic kinase PLK1, STAG1 siRNA reduced cell viability in STAG2-negative bladder cancer cells but had little or no effect on STAG2-positive bladder cancer cell lines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: STAG1 depletion prevented colony formation in STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 but not in STAG2 wild-type UM-UC-5 bladder cancer cells.
source: STAG1 depletion prevented colony formation and abolished sister chromatid cohesion selectively in STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 (F983fs) but not in STAG2 wild-type UM-UC-5 bladder cancer cells (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: STAG1 depletion abolished sister chromatid cohesion selectively in STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 but not in STAG2 wild-type UM-UC-5 bladder cancer cells.
source: STAG1 depletion prevented colony formation and abolished sister chromatid cohesion selectively in STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 (F983fs) but not in STAG2 wild-type UM-UC-5 bladder cancer cells (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SGOL1 depletion abrogated cell growth and cohesion in both STAG2 wild-type and STAG2 mutated bladder cancer cells.
source: In contrast, SGOL1 depletion abrogated cell growth and cohesion in both cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by colony formation and chromosome spread data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: STAG2 mutation status was linked to STAG1 dependency in a panel of four Ewing sarcoma cell lines.
source: Consistent with the results obtained in bladder cancer cells, STAG2 mutation status was also linked to STAG1 dependency in a panel of four Ewing sarcoma cell lines (Figure 3E,F and Supplementary file 2) (Solomon et al., 2011; Tirode et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Lentiviral transduction of a FLAG-STAG2 transgene into STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 bladder cancer cells resulted in the restoration of STAG2 expression.
source: Lentiviral transduction of a FLAG-STAG2 transgene into STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 bladder cancer cells resulted in the restoration of STAG2 expression, nuclear localization of the transgenic protein and its incorporation into the cohesin complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The transgenic FLAG-STAG2 protein localized to the nucleus in UM-UC-3 cells.
source: Lentiviral transduction of a FLAG-STAG2 transgene into STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 bladder cancer cells resulted in the restoration of STAG2 expression, nuclear localization of the transgenic protein and its incorporation into the cohesin complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The transgenic FLAG-STAG2 protein was incorporated into the cohesin complex in UM-UC-3 cells.
source: Lentiviral transduction of a FLAG-STAG2 transgene into STAG2 mutated UM-UC-3 bladder cancer cells resulted in the restoration of STAG2 expression, nuclear localization of the transgenic protein and its incorporation into the cohesin complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing co-precipitation with cohesin subunits in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Restoration of STAG2 expression alleviated the STAG1 dependency of UM-UC-3 cells.
source: Crucially, restoration of STAG2 expression alleviated the STAG1 dependency of UM-UC-3 cells providing a causal link between STAG2 loss and STAG1 dependency (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Restoration of STAG2 expression provides a causal link between STAG2 loss and STAG1 dependency.
source: Crucially, restoration of STAG2 expression alleviated the STAG1 dependency of UM-UC-3 cells providing a causal link between STAG2 loss and STAG1 dependency (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing that restoring STAG2 eliminates STAG1 dependency.

claim: The paralog dependency between STAG1 and STAG2 has recently also been reported in an independent study.
source: The paralog dependency between STAG1 and STAG2 has recently also been reported in an independent study (Benedetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an independent study (Benedetti et al., 2017).

claim: The genetic vulnerability of STAG2 mutant cells to STAG1 loss is not bypassed by transcriptional activation of the germline-specific paralog STAG3.
source: Importantly, the finding that cancer cells harboring deleterious STAG2 mutations remain exquisitely dependent on STAG1 demonstrates that this genetic vulnerability is maintained throughout the process of carcinogenesis and not bypassed by adaptive processes, such as the transcriptional activation of the germline-specific paralog STAG3 (Pezzi et al., 2000; Prieto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that STAG2 mutant cancer cells remain dependent on STAG1, suggesting STAG3 is not compensating.

claim: The loss of sister chromatid cohesion followed by aberrant cell division and cell death is the mechanistic basis underlying the synthetic lethality between STAG1 and STAG2.
source: Our experiments strongly suggest that the loss of sister chromatid cohesion followed by aberrant cell division and cell death is the mechanistic basis underlying the synthetic lethality between STAG1 and STAG2 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental data including cohesion assays, mitotic analysis, and apoptosis measurements.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 associate with the cohesin complex in a mutually exclusive manner.
source: Both paralogs associate with the cohesin complex in a mutually exclusive manner (Losada et al., 2000; Sumara et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Losada et al., 2000; Sumara et al., 2000).

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 containing complexes act redundantly to ensure sufficient sister chromatid cohesion to support cell division in human somatic cells.
source: Although STAG1 and STAG2 may confer distinct functionalities to the cohesin complex (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Remeseiro et al., 2012), STAG1 and STAG2 containing complexes act redundantly to ensure sufficient sister chromatid cohesion to support cell division in human somatic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality data and supported by citations to prior work (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Remeseiro et al., 2012).

claim: While the loss of one STAG paralog is compatible with cell viability and proliferation, the loss of both paralogs abrogates cohesin's ability to hold sister chromatids together, which results in lethality.
source: While the loss of one paralog is compatible with cell viability and proliferation, the loss of both paralogs abrogates cohesin's ability to hold sister chromatids together, which results in lethality.
evidence: This is supported by the synthetic lethality data and mechanistic studies.

claim: Previous studies employed double siRNA depletion experiments to indicate functional redundancy between STAG1 and STAG2 in maintaining sister chromatid cohesion.
source: These mechanistic findings are consistent with previous studies that employed double siRNA depletion experiments to indicate functional redundancy between STAG1 and STAG2 in maintaining sister chromatid cohesion (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Hara et al., 2014; Remeseiro et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Hara et al., 2014; Remeseiro et al., 2012).

claim: STAG1 inactivation has little or no effect on the proliferation of STAG2 proficient cells.
source: Since STAG1 inactivation has little or no effect on the proliferation of STAG2 proficient cells, selective targeting of STAG1 could offer a large therapeutic window.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple STAG2 wild-type cell lines.

claim: Selective targeting of STAG1 could offer a large therapeutic window.
source: Since STAG1 inactivation has little or no effect on the proliferation of STAG2 proficient cells, selective targeting of STAG1 could offer a large therapeutic window.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of STAG1 loss on STAG2 mutant cells.

claim: STAG2 mRNA is expressed in all normal human tissues analyzed.
source: The fact that STAG2 mRNA is expressed in all normal human tissues analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) supports the hypothesis that selective inhibition of STAG1 function would indeed spare most non-cancerous tissues.
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Selective inhibition of STAG1 function would spare most non-cancerous tissues.
source: The fact that STAG2 mRNA is expressed in all normal human tissues analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) supports the hypothesis that selective inhibition of STAG1 function would indeed spare most non-cancerous tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of STAG2 in normal tissues, suggesting they would not depend on STAG1.

claim: Potential approaches for therapeutic targeting of STAG1 include the inhibition of the interaction between STAG1 and the cohesin ring subunit RAD21.
source: Potential approaches for therapeutic targeting of STAG1 include the inhibition of the interaction between STAG1 and the cohesin ring subunit RAD21 (Hara et al., 2014) and the selective degradation of STAG1 using proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) technology (Deshaies, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by citation to prior work (Hara et al., 2014).

claim: Potential approaches for therapeutic targeting of STAG1 include the selective degradation of STAG1 using proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) technology.
source: Potential approaches for therapeutic targeting of STAG1 include the inhibition of the interaction between STAG1 and the cohesin ring subunit RAD21 (Hara et al., 2014) and the selective degradation of STAG1 using proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) technology (Deshaies, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by citation to PROTAC technology (Deshaies, 2015).

claim: The high degree of homology between STAG1 and its paralog STAG2 will be a key challenge to overcome for therapeutic targeting.
source: The high degree of homology between the STAG1 and its paralog STAG2 will be a key challenge to overcome.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of protein targeting challenges.

claim: Knowledge of mechanisms by which mutations in STAG2 and other cohesin subunits drive tumorigenesis is not a prerequisite for the identification of selective vulnerabilities.
source: The mechanisms by which mutations in STAG2 and other cohesin subunits drive tumorigenesis in solid and hematological tissues are not yet firmly established. Our work highlights the fact that such knowledge is not a prerequisite for the identification of selective vulnerabilities.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful identification of STAG1 as a vulnerability without fully understanding the tumorigenic mechanisms.

claim: Both deleterious STAG2 mutations and the loss of STAG2 expression are strong predictive biomarkers for STAG1 dependence in cell models.
source: Both deleterious STAG2 mutations and the loss of STAG2 expression are strong predictive biomarkers for STAG1 dependence in cell models and could be utilized for patient stratification in the future.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple cell line models showing correlation between STAG2 status and STAG1 dependency.

claim: STAG2 status could be utilized for patient stratification in the future.
source: Both deleterious STAG2 mutations and the loss of STAG2 expression are strong predictive biomarkers for STAG1 dependence in cell models and could be utilized for patient stratification in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the predictive value of STAG2 status in cell models.

claim: Unique genetic dependencies of cohesin mutated cancer cells exist.
source: Our work demonstrates that unique genetic dependencies of cohesin mutated cancer cells exist.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of STAG1 as a specific dependency of STAG2 mutant cells.

claim: The genetic dependencies of cohesin mutated cancer cells hold the promise for the development of selective treatments for patients suffering from STAG2 mutated cancer.
source: Such vulnerabilities hold the promise for the development of selective treatments for patients suffering from STAG2 mutated cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the identified synthetic lethality.

claim: In wild-type cells, both cohesin-STAG1 and cohesin-STAG2 complexes redundantly contribute to sister chromatid cohesion and successful cell division.
source: In wild-type cells, both cohesin-STAG1 and cohesin-STAG2 complexes redundantly contribute to sister chromatid cohesion and successful cell division.
evidence: This is shown in the model diagram in Figure 4 and supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of STAG1 is tolerated in wild-type cells as cohesin-STAG2 complexes alone suffice to support sister chromatid cohesion for cell division.
source: Loss of STAG1 is tolerated in these cells as cohesin-STAG2 complexes alone suffice to support sister chromatid cohesion for cell division.
evidence: This is shown in the model diagram in Figure 4 and supported by experimental data from wild-type cells.

claim: In cancer cells in which STAG2 is inactivated, sister chromatid cohesion is entirely dependent on cohesin-STAG1 complexes.
source: In cancer cells in which STAG2 is mutationally or transcriptionally inactivated, sister chromatid cohesion is now entirely dependent on cohesin-STAG1 complexes.
evidence: This is shown in the model diagram in Figure 4 and supported by experimental data from STAG2 mutant cells.

claim: Inactivation of STAG1 in STAG2 mutated cells results in a loss of sister chromatid cohesion followed by mitotic failure and cell death.
source: Inactivation of STAG1 in STAG2 mutated cells therefore results in a loss of sister chromatid cohesion followed by mitotic failure and cell death.
evidence: This is shown in the model diagram in Figure 4 and supported by experimental data.

claim: HCT 116 cells are near-diploid and chromosomally stable.
source: To identify factors whose inactivation would be synthetic lethal with loss of STAG2 function, we first used CRISPR/Cas9 to inactivate STAG2 in near-diploid, chromosomally stable HCT 116 colon carcinoma cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a characterization of the cell line used.

claim: The transgenic FLAG-STAG1 protein was incorporated into the cohesin complex in STAG2- HCT 116 cells.
source: Co-precipitation of cohesin subunits was only detected in FLAG-STAG1 expressing cells indicating specific incorporation of the transgenic protein into the cohesin complex.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: STAG1 and STAG2 may confer distinct functionalities to the cohesin complex.
source: Although STAG1 and STAG2 may confer distinct functionalities to the cohesin complex (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Remeseiro et al., 2012), STAG1 and STAG2 containing complexes act redundantly to ensure sufficient sister chromatid cohesion to support cell division in human somatic cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Canudas and Smith, 2009; Remeseiro et al., 2012).
